subject: hoffman

brief.inclusion: LinkedIn co-founder, venture investor and Democratic megadonor whose political influence connects Silicon Valley capital, candidate networks and AI policy.
brief.namesakes: Matched through Reid Garrett Hoffman, Greylock/LinkedIn affiliations and Bay Area addresses.

coverage.lags: State-party giving, nonprofit grants and litigation support are not all represented in federal Schedule A data.

openQuestions: Some political projects are funded through organizations or advisers rather than personal FEC contributions.
Hoffman's investments and AI-policy advocacy overlap, but investment does not by itself establish control over a company's public position.

summary: Reid Hoffman co-founded LinkedIn, served as a senior PayPal executive and became a partner at Greylock, building wealth and relationships across Silicon Valley. Since 2016 he has also become one of the Democratic Party's largest technology-sector donors, financing candidates, party committees and experimental political organizations while advocating an optimistic, deployment-oriented approach to artificial intelligence.

statements.quote: Networks and marketplaces are central to all of my investing and thinking.

Hoffman apologized for funding the organization behind the Alabama misinformation experiment and said he did not know it would use deceptive tactics.
Hoffman argues that rapid, widespread AI adoption can give individuals more capability and improve collective problem-solving.

chapters.title: Philosophy before platforms
chapters.dek: Hoffman's technical and philosophical education shaped a career focused on how people coordinate through systems.
chapters.body: Raised in the Bay Area, Hoffman studied symbolic systems at Stanford and philosophy at Oxford. He considered academic work but chose technology as a field where ideas about identity, cooperation and institutions could reach large populations. [[greylock-bio, stanford-hoffman, britannica-hoffman]]

chapters.title: SocialNet and PayPal
chapters.dek: Two early companies taught Hoffman that network value depends as much on trust and distribution as on software.
chapters.body: SocialNet was an early attempt to organize real-world relationships online. At PayPal, Hoffman managed external relationships and regulatory problems as the payments company scaled. The experience placed him in a durable network of founders and investors before he built LinkedIn. [[britannica-hoffman, greylock-bio]]

chapters.title: Professional identity as infrastructure
chapters.dek: LinkedIn turned resumes and business relationships into a global platform with strong network effects.
chapters.body: Hoffman co-founded LinkedIn in 2002. Its value grew as workers, recruiters and companies joined the same identity graph; the 2011 public offering and 2016 Microsoft acquisition converted that model into substantial wealth and influence. [[linkedin-history, greylock-bio, microsoft-linkedin]]

chapters.title: From founder to network investor
chapters.dek: At Greylock, Hoffman backed companies whose products become more useful as participation expands.
chapters.body: Joining Greylock in 2009 gave Hoffman a platform across consumer technology, autonomous systems and AI. Board roles and early investments widened a network already built at PayPal and LinkedIn, while books and podcasts made his theory of scaling part of Silicon Valley's public vocabulary. [[greylock-bio, wired-blitzscaling, possible-ai]]

chapters.title: Scaling anti-Trump political giving
chapters.dek: The 2016 election moved Hoffman from conventional donations toward infrastructure, experimentation and opposition strategy.
chapters.body: Hoffman became a major Democratic donor after Trump's election, funding candidates, party committees and organizations intended to improve data and recruitment. His support for Nikki Haley in the 2024 Republican primary illustrated a tactical approach: finance whichever viable route appeared most likely to prevent Trump's return. [[fec-hoffman, wapo-donors, nyt-haley]]

chapters.title: The limits of political experimentation
chapters.dek: A deceptive Alabama project exposed the risks of importing growth-hacking norms into elections.
chapters.body: A 2017 Alabama Senate project used false online personas and tactics designed to resemble Russian interference. Hoffman funded the organization behind it but said he had not known the methods and apologized. The episode remains important because his political model delegated resources to experimental operators whose tactics could undermine the democratic norms they claimed to defend. [[nyt-alabama, hoffman-apology]]

chapters.title: AI investment and technological optimism
chapters.dek: Hoffman argues for rapid deployment while investing directly in companies positioned to benefit from it.
chapters.body: Inflection AI, Greylock investments, podcasts and Superagency place Hoffman on both the commercial and intellectual sides of the AI debate. He emphasizes human agency and learning through use, generally resisting precautionary approaches that would slow deployment. That stance creates a direct policy interest in competition, platform access and regulation. [[inflection-launch, superagency, greylock-bio]]

chapters.title: Capital, access and policy preference
chapters.dek: Hoffman's influence is strongest where venture economics, Democratic fundraising and technology policy meet.
chapters.body: Large donations provide access and organizational leverage; investments create expertise and financial exposure; public commentary shapes elite debate. His 2024 criticism of Lina Khan made those layers visible: a major Democratic supporter asked his preferred administration to change the regulator overseeing technology deals. The request does not prove control, but it shows why his political spending and business interests must be read together. [[cnn-khan, fec-hoffman, opensecrets-2024]]
